title: Effects of four workplace lighting technologies on perception, cognition and affective state
research_question: How do different workplace lighting technologies (fluorescent vs. LED with varied color temperatures and luminances) affect human visual perception, affective state, and cognitive performance?

participants.description: 20 male and 4 female US Army infantry members, aged 18-30 years (Mean: 21.46, SD: 3.1), with normal visual acuity and color vision, stationed at the Natick Soldier Systems Center.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: A climate-controlled Tent Expandable Modular Personnel (TEMPER) military shelter (32' L x 20' 6" W, 640 sq. ft.) insulated for complete darkness, maintained at 70°F. Equipped with one of four lighting technologies per session.
Fluorescent lighting technology with average color temperature of 3345 K (range 3320-3370 K) and general shelter illumination of 20.3 foot candles.
LED 1 lighting technology with average color temperature of 4175 K (range 4140-4210 K) and general shelter illumination of 17.8 foot candles.
LED 2 lighting technology with average color temperature of 5448 K (range 5405-5490 K) and general shelter illumination of 22 foot candles.
LED 3 lighting technology with average color temperature of 6029 K (range 5996-6062 K) and general shelter illumination of 32.6 foot candles.

mechanisms: Increased color temperature (LED) leads to increased arousal, which in turn facilitates faster cognitive processing (reaction times) without necessarily affecting accuracy.
Higher color temperatures (LED) reduce depression and fatigue, and increase vigor/activity, suggesting an enhancement of mood valence and arousal.
Lighting-induced improvements in participant mood state (reduced depression, increased vigor/activity, decreased fatigue) reliably predict faster cognitive task performance.
implementation_implications: LED lighting technologies, particularly those with higher color temperatures, can promote increased alertness and visual cognitive efficiency among workers in industrial settings.
The positive effects of LED lighting on mood and cognitive performance suggest benefits for worker productivity and well-being in temporary military shelters and similar environments.

limitations: Participants were explicitly informed about the study's interest in lighting effects on affect and cognition, which might have influenced results, though they were blind to the color temperature manipulation and physical form factors of the lights.

Participants were exposed to each lighting condition only once, reducing the likelihood that prior expectations influenced subsequent behavior, but daily experiences might have developed preferences for certain lighting types.
